items.label: section_header
items.text: WORKING OUT A NUMBER OF MOLES FROM A VOLUME AND A CONCENTRATION

items.label: section_header
items.text: A CALCULATION INVOLVING HARD WATER

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Don't be scared that some of this is new to you! As long as you realise that CHCOOH is ethanoic acid, that's all you need to worry about for this calculation.

items.label: text
items.text: When doing calculations involving solutions you will most often be asked to calculate a number of moles given the volume of the solution and its concentration. The equation for doing this is:

items.label: text
items.text: number of moles = volume of solution (dm³) × concentration (mol/dm³)

items.label: text
items.text: Because concentration is usually given in units of mol/dm³ but volumes of solutions are often given in cm³, we usually have to convert the volume in cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXAMPLE3

items.label: text
items.text: Calculate the number of moles of NaOH in 50 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ solution.

items.label: text
items.text: Converting the volume to dm³ we get 50/1000 = 0.050 dm³.

items.label: text
items.text: Number of moles = volume of solution (dm³) × concentration (mol/dm³).

items.label: text
items.text: Number of moles = 0.050 × 0.10 = 0.0050 mol.

items.label: section_header
items.text: CALCULATIONS WITH EQUATIONS INVOLVING SOLUTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: Limescale can be removed from, for example, electric kettles by reacting it with a dilute acid such as ethanoic acid, which is present in vinegar:

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } ( s ) + 2 C H _ { 3 } C O O H ( a q ) \rightarrow ( O H _ { 3 } C O O ) _ { 2 } C a ( a q ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: text
items.text: What mass of calcium carbonate can be removed by 50 cm³ of a solution of ethanoic acid that has a concentration of 2 mol/dm³?

items.label: text
items.text: Again, we will use our three stages:

items.label: list_item
items.text: calculate the number of moles of what we can

items.label: list_item
items.text: use the chemical equation to work out the number of moles of what we want

items.label: list_item
items.text: convert the number of moles to what is required in the question.

items.label: text
items.text: We know the volume and concentration of ethanoic acid and so we can calculate the number of moles of ethanoic acid:

items.label: text
items.text: number of moles = volume of solution (dm³) × concentration (mol/dm3)

items.label: text
items.text: We need to be careful to convert the volume of ethanoic acid to dm³ by dividing by 1000:

items.label: formula
items.text: \text {number of moles of ethanoi acid} = \frac { 5 0 } { 1 0 0 0 } \times 2 = 0 , 1 \, m o l

items.label: text
items.text: From the chemical equation we can see that there is a 2 in front of the CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) but no number (which means a 1) in front of the CaCO3, so we can deduce that 2 mol of CHgCOOH react with 1 mol of CaCO3, in other words the number of moles of CaCO3is half the number of moles of CH3COOH. Therefore, we can deduce that 0.1 mol of ethanoic acid will react with 0.1/2 = 0.05 mol of CaCO.

items.label: text
items.text: We can now calculate the mass of CaCO3 (M, = 100):

items.label: text
items.text: mass = number of moles × mass of 1 mol = 0.05 × 100 = 5g

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore the ethanoic acid reacts with 5g of calcium carbonate.
